supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and Einstein tensor $G$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]), let
$\Sigma\subseteq M$ be a spacelike embedded hypersurface
([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]],
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (a)), and fix real
constants $\kappa$ and $\Lambda$ (the framework coupling constants, purely
parameters for this definition).

**(a) The geometric data.**
For $p\in\Sigma$ the orthogonal complement $T_p\Sigma^{\perp}$ is
one-dimensional and nondegenerate
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]); there is therefore a unique
$n_p\in T_p\Sigma^{\perp}$ with $g_p(n_p,n_p)=-1$ and $g_p(n_p,N_p)<0$ and it
depends smoothly on $p$, the **future unit normal field** of $\Sigma$; this
and the properties of $h$ and $K$ below are proved, not assumed, in
[[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]]. Define
on $\Sigma$ the **induced metric** $h$ and the **second fundamental form**
$K$ by
$$h_p(V,W):=g_p(V,W),\qquad K_p(V,W):=g_p(\nabla_Vn,W)\qquad(V,W\in T_p\Sigma),$$
where $\nabla_Vn$ is the covariant derivative at $p$ of the ambient field $n$
in the tangential direction $V$; $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric on
$\Sigma$ and $K$ a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $\Sigma$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]).

**(b) Matter data and constraints.** Let $T$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $M$ (the stress-energy field of a matter branch). Its
**matter data on $\Sigma$** are the smooth fields
$$\rho:=T(n,n),\qquad j(V):=-T(n,V)\quad(V\in T\Sigma).$$
The tuple $(\Sigma,h,K,\rho,j)$ **satisfies the constraint equations** for
$(\kappa,\Lambda)$ when
$$G(n,n)-\Lambda=\kappa\,\rho,\qquad G(n,V)=\kappa\,T(n,V)\quad\text{for every }V\in T_p\Sigma,\ p\in\Sigma .$$
The first is the normal projection of the equation $G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$
evaluated on $(n,n)$, namely $G(n,n)+\Lambda g(n,n)=\kappa T(n,n)$, with
$g(n,n)=-1$; the second is the normal-tangential projection, the term in
$\Lambda$ dropping because $g(n,V)=0$. That a solution of the field equation
satisfies these two projections is proved in
[[lem-gr-constraint-projections]]. The purely tangential projection
$G(V,W)+\Lambda h(V,W)=\kappa T(V,W)$ is not part of the constraints and is
not required here.

**(c) Developments.** A **development** of the data
$(\Sigma,h,K,\rho,j)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
$(M',g',N')$ together with a smooth embedding $\varphi:\Sigma\to M'$ whose
image is a spacelike embedded hypersurface with induced metric $\varphi^*g'=h$
and second fundamental form $K$ with respect to its future unit normal $n'$.
Write $T'$ for the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field included as
the development's stress-energy field. Require the tensor equation
$$G'+\Lambda g'=\kappa T'$$
at every point of $M'$, where $G'$ is the Einstein tensor of $g'$ with its
metric-selected connection, defined as above. The constants $\kappa$ and
$\Lambda$ are the fixed parameters of the initial data. The matter-data matching condition is
the pair of normal projections
$$\rho(p)=T'_{\varphi(p)}(n'_{\varphi(p)},n'_{\varphi(p)}),\qquad j_p(V)=-T'_{\varphi(p)}(n'_{\varphi(p)},d\varphi_p(V))\quad(p\in\Sigma,\ V\in T_p\Sigma).$$
Equivalently, the scalar field $T'(n',n')$ along $\varphi(\Sigma)$ pulls
back to $\rho$, and the covector field $-T'(n',\cdot)$ restricted to
$T\varphi(\Sigma)$ pulls back to $j$. This tuple prescribes only these
stress-energy projections; any additional matter-field data are not included
in $(\Sigma,h,K,\rho,j)$. The development is a **globally hyperbolic
development** when
$\varphi(\Sigma)$ is a Cauchy hypersurface of $(M',g',N')$. The implication
from this Cauchy property to global hyperbolicity of $(M',g',N')$ is a
separate theorem, deferred to the later causal theory; it is not established
by this definition
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]],
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c)).

**(d) Maximality.** A globally hyperbolic development $(M_*,g_*,N_*;
\varphi_*)$ is **maximal** for the data when for every globally hyperbolic
development $(M',g',N';\varphi')$ there is a smooth isometric embedding
$\psi:M'\to M_*$ with $\psi\circ\varphi'=\varphi_*$, $\psi$ preserving the
time orientations and carrying the selected stress-energy tensor $T'$ to
$T_*$, that is, $\psi^*T_*=T'$. This is a universal embedding property: every globally hyperbolic
development embeds into the selected maximal one with its data and
stress-energy tensor preserved. It does not assert that arbitrary globally
hyperbolic developments are mutually isometric.

**(e) Scope.** The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of
developments, and it does not assert that $T'$ is generated by matter fields
solving any equation: those claims require the local and global existence theory of
the Einstein-matter system and are not made on this page. The constraint
equations are displayed only as equations satisfied or not by given data.
The equivalent formulation of the constraints in terms of the induced scalar
curvature of $h$ and the divergence of $K$, and the existence theory for
solutions of the constraints, rest on the Gauss-Codazzi relations and on PDE
theory and are deferred to the later pages of this track; no such
equivalence is asserted here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, and let $\Sigma\subseteq M$ be a smooth spacelike embedded hypersurface with future unit normal $n$, induced Riemannian metric $h$ and second fundamental form $K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$ ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], [[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]]). Write $D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $h$, $R^h$ for its curvature operator in the same operator convention as the ambient curvature, and $S_h$ for its scalar curvature. Explicitly distinguish the lowered tensor from the operator pairing by setting
$$\mathcal R^g(A,B,C,D):=g(R^g(C,D)B,A),\qquad \mathcal R^h(A,B,C,D):=h(R^h(C,D)B,A).$$
Thus $\mathcal R^g_{abcd}=R_{abcd}$ in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]; in particular $g(R^g(X,Y)Z,W)=\mathcal R^g(W,Z,X,Y)$. Let $G$ be the Einstein tensor defined there. At every $p\in\Sigma$ and for all $X,Y,Z,W\in T_p\Sigma$:

**(a) Gauss equation.**
$$\mathcal R^g(X,Y,Z,W)=\mathcal R^h(X,Y,Z,W)+K(X,Z)K(Y,W)-K(X,W)K(Y,Z).$$
Equivalently, in operator order,
$$g(R^g(X,Y)Z,W)=h(R^h(X,Y)Z,W)+K(Y,Z)K(X,W)-K(X,Z)K(Y,W).$$

**(b) Codazzi equation.**
$$g(R^g(X,Y)Z,n)=(D_YK)(X,Z)-(D_XK)(Y,Z).$$

**(c) Normal projections.** Define $(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)=h^{ij}(D_{e_i}K)(e_j,Y)$, $\tau=\operatorname{tr}_hK=h^{ij}K_{ij}$ and $|K|_h^2=h^{ik}h^{jl}K_{ij}K_{kl}$. Then
$$G(n,n)=\tfrac12(S_h+\tau^2-|K|_h^2),\qquad G(n,Y)=(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau.$$

**(d) Constraint equations.** If the tensor equation $G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ holds at $p$, for a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor $T$ and real constants $\kappa,\Lambda$, then
$$S_h+\tau^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T(n,n),\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau=\kappa T(n,Y).$$
With $\rho=T(n,n)$ and $j(Y)=-T(n,Y)$, the second equation is $(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau=-\kappa j(Y)$.

In coordinates for a Riemannian metric with matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, its Levi–Civita symbols are
$$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12\sum_\ell g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_j g_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij}).$$

Riemannian metric $m$ in coordinates,
$\Gamma[m]^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12m^{k\ell}(\partial_i m_{j\ell}
+\partial_jm_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell m_{ij})$.

For a supplied Riemannian metric $g$, a **Levi–Civita connection** is an affine connection on $TM$ that is both metric compatible and torsion free, in the senses of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], [[def-metric-compatible-connection-on-a-riemannian-vector-bundle]] and [[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]]. Thus for all local fields
$$Xg(Y,Z)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ),\qquad 
abla_XY-
abla_YX=[X,Y].$$
Existence and uniqueness are proved below from the supplied metric by the Koszul formula. This definition does not choose an arbitrary connection first and does not assume the general connection-existence theorem. In dimension zero the unique tangent-bundle connection satisfies both identities; in dimension one torsion freeness alone imposes no restriction, so metric compatibility remains essential.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **dual connection** on the smooth bundle $E^*$ of [[def-connection-on-a-smooth-vector-bundle]] is characterized by
$$ (\nabla^*_X\alpha)(s)=X(\alpha(s))-\alpha(\nabla_Xs).$$
The right side is function-linear in $s$: replacing $s$ by $fs$ introduces $X(f)\alpha(s)$ once with each sign, so those terms cancel.

Here is the construction, including well-definedness. In a frame $e$ write $s=eu$ and write $\alpha$ with dual coefficient column $a$, so $\alpha(s)=a^Tu$. The coordinate formula [[prop-local-coordinate-formula-for-a-bundle-connection]] gives
$$X(a^Tu)-a^T(X(u)+\omega(X)u)=(X(a)-\omega(X)^Ta)^Tu.$$
Thus the required coefficients are $X(a)-\omega(X)^Ta$, and the local connection matrix in the dual frame is $-\omega^T$. These local rules are smooth, real-linear and obey the section Leibniz rule by the scalar product rule. On an overlap both give the intrinsic displayed pairing formula; agreement against every local frame section forces equality of the dual covectors. They therefore glue to a connection, equivalently by [[thm-local-connection-forms-glue-exactly-when-they-obey-the-transformation-law]]. Testing against a basis also proves uniqueness. This verifies the implicit characterization rather than assuming that it defines an operator.

The derivative on scalar functions is $X(f)$; duality preserves the evaluation pairing with that scalar connection. For rank one the matrix changes sign; for rank zero evaluation and all coefficients are empty. Zero sections give zero derivatives, while empty bases give the unique operator. This construction is local and canonical from the given connection and requires no choice axiom.

[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]]: the induced covariant
derivative on dual and tensor-product bundles obeys the dual-pairing and
Leibniz rules, so a metric-compatible connection also annihilates the inverse
metric.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Give each of finitely many bundles $E_j$ a connection. Use the tensor bundle constructed in [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]], including its multilinear model on the dual fibres. The **product connection** is characterized on local elementary tensors by
$$\nabla_X(s_1\otimes\cdots\otimes s_k)=\sum_j s_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\nabla^j_Xs_j\otimes\cdots\otimes s_k.$$
For the empty product, the connection on scalar functions is $\nabla_Xf=X(f)$.

To construct it without a decomposition assumption, for a multilinear-model section $T$ and local dual sections $\alpha_j$ put
$$(\nabla_XT)(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)=X\bigl(T(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)\bigr)-\sum_jT(\alpha_1,\ldots,(\nabla^j)^*_X\alpha_j,\ldots,\alpha_k).$$
Use the dual connections of [[def-dual-connection]]. Multiplying any argument by a smooth $f$ produces two opposite $X(f)T(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ terms; thus this expression is function-linear in every dual argument. In dual frames its coefficients are smooth and depend only on their fibre values, so it defines a smooth tensor section. The same intrinsic expression on overlaps gives agreement. Its real-linearity, function-linearity in $X$, and rule $\nabla_X(fT)=X(f)T+f\nabla_XT$ follow by direct expansion, establishing the connection. This also gives the gluing criterion of [[thm-local-connection-forms-glue-exactly-when-they-obey-the-transformation-law]].

On a pure tensor, the scalar product rule and the dual pairing identity reduce this expression to the first displayed sum. Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
(Ordered field, Field).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of Laws of integer exponents: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors (A field has no zero divisors: $ab = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$ or $b = 0$).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
(Identities and inverses in a field are unique).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ (The integers as equivalence classes of pairs of naturals) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ (The naturals embed in the integers,
Arithmetic on the integers). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total (The integers form a totally ordered ring), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ (The naturals embed in the integers); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition (The integers form a totally ordered ring),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty smooth three-manifold without boundary that is
**compact**: for every family $(U_a)_{a\in A}$ of open subsets of $\Sigma$
with $\Sigma=\bigcup_{a\in A}U_a$, there is a finite subset $F\subseteq A$
such that $\Sigma=\bigcup_{a\in F}U_a$. In this item, “vacuum” means that the stress-energy tensor is zero and the
cosmological constant is fixed at $\Lambda=0$. Let $\widetilde h$ be a smooth
Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\widetilde\sigma$ be a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor field, let $\tau\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and let
$\phi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\phi(p)>0$ at every $p\in\Sigma$.
Use the positive scalar $\phi$ as a dimensionless conformal factor.

Write $\widetilde D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $\widetilde h$ and
$D$ for that of the metric $h$ defined below. On covariant tensor fields, these
symbols also denote their induced product connections, with the dual and
tensor-factor rules of the product-connection supplier in Definition references.
In a chart, $\widetilde h^{ij}$
denotes the inverse matrix to $\widetilde h_{ij}$. It is smooth because
$\det(\widetilde h_{ij})>0$ and the matrix inverse is the adjugate divided by
the determinant. For any smooth Riemannian metric $m$ on $\Sigma$, with
Levi-Civita connection $D^m$, define
$$R^m(X,Y)Z:=D^m_XD^m_YZ-D^m_YD^m_XZ-D^m_{[X,Y]}Z.$$
In a chart, $R[m]^a{}_{bij}$ denotes the components of
$R^m(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_b$. Define
$\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}:=R[m]^k{}_{ikj}$ and
$R(m):=m^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}$. In particular,
$\widetilde R:=R(\widetilde h)$, with the same curvature sign convention.
Define the scalar Laplacian by
$$\widetilde\Delta f:=\widetilde h^{ij} (\partial_i\partial_j f-\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k f),$$
where $\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ are the Christoffel symbols of
$\widetilde D$, given by the Levi-Civita Christoffel formula
in Definition references.
The curvature sign is the one displayed above. All traces, norms, raising of
indices and contractions in this item use the metric indicated by the
subscript. In particular,
$$\operatorname{tr}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma:=\widetilde h^{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{ij},\qquad |\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde h^{j\ell}\widetilde\sigma_{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma)_j:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde D_i\widetilde\sigma_{kj}.$$
The tensor $\widetilde\sigma$ is **transverse-traceless** (TT) with respect
to $\widetilde h$ when it is symmetric and both displayed trace and divergence
vanish. The input tensor in this definition is required to be TT.

Define
$$h:=\phi^4\widetilde h,\qquad K:=\phi^{-2}\widetilde\sigma+\frac{\tau}{3}h.$$
Because $\phi>0$, $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric; because
$\widetilde\sigma$ and $h$ are symmetric, $K$ is a smooth symmetric tensor.
Here $h$ is the candidate induced Riemannian metric and $K$ is the candidate
second fundamental form, with the library convention
$K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X n,Y)$ when the data are induced by a spacelike hypersurface
with future unit normal $n$. The pair is **vacuum conformal constraint data**.
It is abstract data on $\Sigma$; no embedding into a spacetime is part of this
definition. For its embedded Lorentzian interpretation assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the supplied smooth tangent-bundle
convention; the algebraic tensor definitions themselves use no choice
principle. Define the $h$-trace, squared norm and divergence by
$$\operatorname{tr}_hK:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|_h^2:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)_j:=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}.$$
With $R(h)$ computed using $h$, define the Hamiltonian and momentum residuals
$$\mathcal H(h,K):=R(h)+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2,\qquad \mathcal M_j(h,K):=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}-D_j(\operatorname{tr}_hK).$$
The data satisfy the vacuum constraint equations when
$\mathcal H(h,K)=0$ and $\mathcal M(h,K)=0$. For an embedded hypersurface,
these are the normal and normal-tangential Einstein constraints in the
specified $K$ convention.

Tensoriality of curvature and basis-independent contraction make these scalar
curvatures independent of the chart.
For dimensional bookkeeping in the SI length convention, $[\tau]=\mathrm m^{-1}$,
$[R(h)]=[\widetilde R]=[|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2]
=[\widetilde\Delta]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $[\phi]=1$. Thus all terms in the
scalar constraint equation have units $\mathrm m^{-2}$.

=[\widetilde\Delta]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $[\phi]=1$. Thus all terms in the

Let $(h,K)$ be the vacuum conformal constraint data of the definition. Then
$\operatorname{tr}_hK=\tau$ and the momentum residual vanishes:
$$\mathcal M_j(h,K)=0.$$
The Hamiltonian residual is
$$\mathcal H(h,K)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -8\widetilde\Delta\phi+\widetilde R\,\phi-|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2\phi^{-7} +\frac{2}{3}\tau^2\phi^5=0.$$
The displayed scalar equation is the **Lichnerowicz equation** for these
constant-mean-curvature (CMC) vacuum data. Here CMC means that the trace
$\operatorname{tr}_hK$ is spatially constant; its value is $\tau$.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

derivations.claim:
For a constant $\phi>0$, $\widetilde\Delta\phi=0$. Substituting
$\widetilde R=0$ and $|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2=A$ in [F2], its
equation becomes $-A\phi^{-7}+(2/3)\tau^2\phi^5=0$. Multiplication by
$\phi^7>0$ is reversible, so this is equivalent to
$\phi^{12}=3A/(2\tau^2)$.

The right side $3A/(2\tau^2)$ is positive because $A>0$ and $\tau\ne0$.
By [F3], it has exactly one positive twelfth root, and by [F4] that root is
$(3A/(2\tau^2))^{1/12}$. Thus this is the unique positive constant solution.

Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty smooth three-manifold without boundary that is
**compact**: for every family $(U_a)_{a\in A}$ of open subsets of $\Sigma$
with $\Sigma=\bigcup_{a\in A}U_a$, there is a finite subset $F\subseteq A$
such that $\Sigma=\bigcup_{a\in F}U_a$. In this item, “vacuum” means that the stress-energy tensor is zero and the
cosmological constant is fixed at $\Lambda=0$. Let $\widetilde h$ be a smooth
Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\widetilde\sigma$ be a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor field, let $\tau\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and let
$\phi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\phi(p)>0$ at every $p\in\Sigma$.
Use the positive scalar $\phi$ as a dimensionless conformal factor.

Write $\widetilde D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $\widetilde h$ and
$D$ for that of the metric $h$ defined below. On covariant tensor fields, these
symbols also denote their induced product connections, with the dual and
tensor-factor rules of the product-connection supplier in Definition references.
In a chart, $\widetilde h^{ij}$
denotes the inverse matrix to $\widetilde h_{ij}$. It is smooth because
$\det(\widetilde h_{ij})>0$ and the matrix inverse is the adjugate divided by
the determinant. For any smooth Riemannian metric $m$ on $\Sigma$, with
Levi-Civita connection $D^m$, define
$$R^m(X,Y)Z:=D^m_XD^m_YZ-D^m_YD^m_XZ-D^m_{[X,Y]}Z.$$
In a chart, $R[m]^a{}_{bij}$ denotes the components of
$R^m(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_b$. Define
$\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}:=R[m]^k{}_{ikj}$ and
$R(m):=m^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}$. In particular,
$\widetilde R:=R(\widetilde h)$, with the same curvature sign convention.
Define the scalar Laplacian by
$$\widetilde\Delta f:=\widetilde h^{ij} (\partial_i\partial_j f-\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k f),$$
where $\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ are the Christoffel symbols of
$\widetilde D$, given by the Levi-Civita Christoffel formula
in Definition references.
The curvature sign is the one displayed above. All traces, norms, raising of
indices and contractions in this item use the metric indicated by the
subscript. In particular,
$$\operatorname{tr}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma:=\widetilde h^{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{ij},\qquad |\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde h^{j\ell}\widetilde\sigma_{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma)_j:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde D_i\widetilde\sigma_{kj}.$$
The tensor $\widetilde\sigma$ is **transverse-traceless** (TT) with respect
to $\widetilde h$ when it is symmetric and both displayed trace and divergence
vanish. The input tensor in this definition is required to be TT.

Define
$$h:=\phi^4\widetilde h,\qquad K:=\phi^{-2}\widetilde\sigma+\frac{\tau}{3}h.$$
Because $\phi>0$, $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric; because
$\widetilde\sigma$ and $h$ are symmetric, $K$ is a smooth symmetric tensor.
Here $h$ is the candidate induced Riemannian metric and $K$ is the candidate
second fundamental form, with the library convention
$K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X n,Y)$ when the data are induced by a spacelike hypersurface
with future unit normal $n$. The pair is **vacuum conformal constraint data**.
It is abstract data on $\Sigma$; no embedding into a spacetime is part of this
definition. For its embedded Lorentzian interpretation assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the supplied smooth tangent-bundle
convention; the algebraic tensor definitions themselves use no choice
principle. Define the $h$-trace, squared norm and divergence by
$$\operatorname{tr}_hK:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|_h^2:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)_j:=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}.$$

$\mathcal H(h,K)=0$ and $\mathcal M(h,K)=0$. For an embedded hypersurface,
these are the normal and normal-tangential Einstein constraints in the
specified $K$ convention.

curvatures independent of the chart.

$[R(h)]=[\widetilde R]=[|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2]
=[\widetilde\Delta]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $[\phi]=1$. Thus all terms in the
scalar constraint equation have units $\mathrm m^{-2}$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(h,K)$ be the vacuum conformal constraint data of the definition. Then
$\operatorname{tr}_hK=\tau$ and the momentum residual vanishes:
$$\mathcal M_j(h,K)=0.$$
The Hamiltonian residual is
$$\mathcal H(h,K)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -8\widetilde\Delta\phi+\widetilde R\,\phi-|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2\phi^{-7} +\frac{2}{3}\tau^2\phi^5=0.$$
The displayed scalar equation is the **Lichnerowicz equation** for these
constant-mean-curvature (CMC) vacuum data. Here CMC means that the trace
$\operatorname{tr}_hK$ is spatially constant; its value is $\tau$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

$x^{1/12}$ denotes its unique positive twelfth root.

clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of maps
$u:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb R^N$ whose pullbacks
$\widetilde u:=u\circ q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ are smooth;
these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when $N=1$).
Equivalently every smooth map $\widetilde u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$
that is $2\pi$-periodic in each coordinate descends to the unique map
$u([x])=\widetilde u(x)$, since periodicity makes this value independent of
$x$ in its equivalence class. For an integer $m\ge0$, define
$C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ similarly by requiring
$\widetilde u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$
([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), and define
$D^\alpha u([x]):=D^\alpha\widetilde u(x)$ for $|\alpha|\le m$.
Derivatives of a periodic $C^m$ map are periodic, so these values are
well-defined, with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}|(D^\alpha u)(x)|,$$
where the multi-index derivative is that of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]].

$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$

$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$

([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when the representative $G(t,x,u):=F(t,q(x),u)$ is
locally the restriction of a smooth Euclidean map: for every
$(t,x,u)\in I\times\mathbb R^3\times O$ there are an open neighborhood

it is the local extension convention at included endpoints, also admitting
a singleton interval. On a nondegenerate interval endpoint time derivatives
are the limits of interior derivatives; on a singleton no time derivative
is specified without choosing an extension. Throughout this page the torus is always this

$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge0$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

**(a)** Let $u\in H^s$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\alpha|\le s$. Then

$$\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\,\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3),\qquad (ik)^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3(ik_j)^{\alpha_j}.$$

**(b)** Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy $N_s(u)<\infty$.

Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty smooth three-manifold without boundary that is
**compact**: for every family $(U_a)_{a\in A}$ of open subsets of $\Sigma$
with $\Sigma=\bigcup_{a\in A}U_a$, there is a finite subset $F\subseteq A$
such that $\Sigma=\bigcup_{a\in F}U_a$. In this item, “vacuum” means that the stress-energy tensor is zero and the
cosmological constant is fixed at $\Lambda=0$. Let $\widetilde h$ be a smooth
Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\widetilde\sigma$ be a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor field, let $\tau\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and let
$\phi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\phi(p)>0$ at every $p\in\Sigma$.
Use the positive scalar $\phi$ as a dimensionless conformal factor.

Write $\widetilde D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $\widetilde h$ and
$D$ for that of the metric $h$ defined below. On covariant tensor fields, these
symbols also denote their induced product connections, with the dual and
tensor-factor rules of the product-connection supplier in Definition references.
In a chart, $\widetilde h^{ij}$
denotes the inverse matrix to $\widetilde h_{ij}$. It is smooth because
$\det(\widetilde h_{ij})>0$ and the matrix inverse is the adjugate divided by
the determinant. For any smooth Riemannian metric $m$ on $\Sigma$, with
Levi-Civita connection $D^m$, define
$$R^m(X,Y)Z:=D^m_XD^m_YZ-D^m_YD^m_XZ-D^m_{[X,Y]}Z.$$
In a chart, $R[m]^a{}_{bij}$ denotes the components of
$R^m(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_b$. Define
$\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}:=R[m]^k{}_{ikj}$ and
$R(m):=m^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}$. In particular,
$\widetilde R:=R(\widetilde h)$, with the same curvature sign convention.
Define the scalar Laplacian by
$$\widetilde\Delta f:=\widetilde h^{ij} (\partial_i\partial_j f-\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k f),$$
where $\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ are the Christoffel symbols of
$\widetilde D$, given by the Levi-Civita Christoffel formula
in Definition references.
The curvature sign is the one displayed above. All traces, norms, raising of
indices and contractions in this item use the metric indicated by the
subscript. In particular,
$$\operatorname{tr}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma:=\widetilde h^{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{ij},\qquad |\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde h^{j\ell}\widetilde\sigma_{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma)_j:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde D_i\widetilde\sigma_{kj}.$$
The tensor $\widetilde\sigma$ is **transverse-traceless** (TT) with respect
to $\widetilde h$ when it is symmetric and both displayed trace and divergence
vanish. The input tensor in this definition is required to be TT.

Define
$$h:=\phi^4\widetilde h,\qquad K:=\phi^{-2}\widetilde\sigma+\frac{\tau}{3}h.$$
Because $\phi>0$, $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric; because
$\widetilde\sigma$ and $h$ are symmetric, $K$ is a smooth symmetric tensor.
Here $h$ is the candidate induced Riemannian metric and $K$ is the candidate
second fundamental form, with the library convention
$K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X n,Y)$ when the data are induced by a spacelike hypersurface
with future unit normal $n$. The pair is **vacuum conformal constraint data**.
It is abstract data on $\Sigma$; no embedding into a spacetime is part of this
definition. For its embedded Lorentzian interpretation assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the supplied smooth tangent-bundle
convention; the algebraic tensor definitions themselves use no choice
principle. Define the $h$-trace, squared norm and divergence by
$$\operatorname{tr}_hK:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|_h^2:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)_j:=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}.$$
With $R(h)$ computed using $h$, define the Hamiltonian and momentum residuals
$$\mathcal H(h,K):=R(h)+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2,\qquad \mathcal M_j(h,K):=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}-D_j(\operatorname{tr}_hK).$$
The data satisfy the vacuum constraint equations when
$\mathcal H(h,K)=0$ and $\mathcal M(h,K)=0$. For an embedded hypersurface,
these are the normal and normal-tangential Einstein constraints in the
specified $K$ convention.

Tensoriality of curvature and basis-independent contraction make these scalar
curvatures independent of the chart.
For dimensional bookkeeping in the SI length convention, $[\tau]=\mathrm m^{-1}$,
$[R(h)]=[\widetilde R]=[|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2]
=[\widetilde\Delta]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $[\phi]=1$. Thus all terms in the
scalar constraint equation have units $\mathrm m^{-2}$.

Let $(h,K)$ be the vacuum conformal constraint data of the definition. Then
$\operatorname{tr}_hK=\tau$ and the momentum residual vanishes:
$$\mathcal M_j(h,K)=0.$$
The Hamiltonian residual is
$$\mathcal H(h,K)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -8\widetilde\Delta\phi+\widetilde R\,\phi-|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2\phi^{-7} +\frac{2}{3}\tau^2\phi^5=0.$$
The displayed scalar equation is the **Lichnerowicz equation** for these
constant-mean-curvature (CMC) vacuum data. Here CMC means that the trace
$\operatorname{tr}_hK$ is spatially constant; its value is $\tau$.

Suppose the conformal metric has $\widetilde R=0$ and
$|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2=A$ is a positive constant, with constant
$\tau\ne0$. Then the Lichnerowicz equation has exactly one positive constant
solution,
$$\phi_0=\left(\frac{3A}{2\tau^2}\right)^{1/12}.$$
With a fixed length unit, $[A]=[\tau^2]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, so $\phi_0$ is
dimensionless. Uniqueness is only among positive constant solutions; no
uniqueness claim is made for arbitrary positive functions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of maps
$u:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb R^N$ whose pullbacks
$\widetilde u:=u\circ q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ are smooth;
these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when $N=1$).
Equivalently every smooth map $\widetilde u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$
that is $2\pi$-periodic in each coordinate descends to the unique map
$u([x])=\widetilde u(x)$, since periodicity makes this value independent of
$x$ in its equivalence class. For an integer $m\ge0$, define
$C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ similarly by requiring
$\widetilde u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$
([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), and define
$D^\alpha u([x]):=D^\alpha\widetilde u(x)$ for $|\alpha|\le m$.
Derivatives of a periodic $C^m$ map are periodic, so these values are
well-defined, with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}|(D^\alpha u)(x)|,$$
where the multi-index derivative is that of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]].

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when the representative $G(t,x,u):=F(t,q(x),u)$ is
locally the restriction of a smooth Euclidean map: for every
$(t,x,u)\in I\times\mathbb R^3\times O$ there are an open neighborhood
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^{4+m}$ and $\widetilde G\in C^\infty(V;\mathbb R^{m'})$
with $\widetilde G=G$ on $V\cap(I\times\mathbb R^3\times O)$.
For open $I$ this is the ordinary Euclidean definition. For nonopen $I$
it is the local extension convention at included endpoints, also admitting
a singleton interval. On a nondegenerate interval endpoint time derivatives
are the limits of interior derivatives; on a singleton no time derivative
is specified without choosing an extension. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge0$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

**(a)** Let $u\in H^s$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\alpha|\le s$. Then
$D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$ and
$$\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\,\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3),\qquad (ik)^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3(ik_j)^{\alpha_j}.$$

**(b)** Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy $N_s(u)<\infty$.
Then $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$, and there are constants
$0<c_s\le C_s<\infty$, depending only on $s$, such that
$$c_s\,N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le C_s\,N_s(u)^2 .$$
The right-hand inequality holds for every $u\in H^s$, so the two norms are
equivalent on $H^s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim:
For a fixed smooth real direction $v$, its periodic lift is continuous on
the nonempty compact box $[0,2\pi]^3$ by [F4, F7], so [F8] gives a finite
bound $V:=\sup|v|$. If $V>0$, choose $|\epsilon|<\phi_0/(2V)$; if $V=0$,
positivity is immediate. In either case $\phi_0+\epsilon v>0$ for all such
directions and sufficiently small $|\epsilon|$.
Every term in $c$ is positive because $A>0$, $\phi_0>0$ and $\tau\ne0$.
Since $\widetilde h_{ij}=L_*^2\delta_{ij}$, the Christoffel formula in the
conformal-data definition gives $\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=0$ in the local
periodic charts. The curvature definition then gives $\widetilde R=0$, and
the Laplacian formula gives $\widetilde\Delta=L_*^{-2}\sum_i\partial_i^2$.
Differentiating the scalar expression [F2] at the constant $\phi_0$ gives
$-8\widetilde\Delta v$ from its linear Laplacian term, zero from
$\widetilde R=0$, $7A\phi_0^{-8}v$ from $-A\phi^{-7}$, and
$(10/3)\tau^2\phi_0^4v$ from $(2/3)\tau^2\phi^5$. Thus its directional
linearization is $\mathcal A=-8\widetilde\Delta+c$. For each $i$,
periodicity makes the integral of $\partial_i(v\partial_i v)$ over one period zero;
expanding that derivative gives
$\int v\partial_i^2v\,d\mu=-\int(\partial_i v)^2\,d\mu$. Summing over $i$
therefore yields
$$\int v\mathcal A v\,d\mu =8L_*^{-2}\int|\nabla_0v|^2\,d\mu+c\int v^2\,d\mu>0$$
for every nonzero smooth real $v$: choose a point where $v\ne0$; continuity
gives a coordinate box of positive torus measure on which $|v|$ is bounded
below by a positive constant, so $\int v^2d\mu>0$. Here
$\nabla_0v=(\partial_1v,\partial_2v,\partial_3v)$.

For any $v\in H^{s+2}$, the weak-derivative Fourier identity [F5] gives
$\widehat{\mathcal A v}(k)=a_k\widehat v(k)$ with
$a_k=8L_*^{-2}|k|^2+c$. Since $c>0$, every $a_k>0$, and
$a_k\ge m(1+|k|^2)$ for
$m:=\min\{8L_*^{-2},c\}>0$; also
$a_k\le M(1+|k|^2)$ for
$M:=\max\{8L_*^{-2},c\}$. The upper bound proves
$N_s(\mathcal A v)\le M N_{s+2}(v)$. Norm equivalence in [F5] therefore
makes the weak operator bounded for the derivative Sobolev norms. For real
$f\in H^s$,
[F6] gives $\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$. Since $a_{-k}=a_k$ is real,
$\widehat v(k):=\widehat f(k)/a_k$ has the same conjugate symmetry and
therefore [F6] gives it a unique complex $L^2$ representative $v$. The
coefficient definition gives $\widehat{\overline v}(k)=\overline{\widehat v(-k)}
=\widehat v(k)$, so injectivity of the coefficient isometry [F6] yields
$\overline v=v$ in $L^2$. The lower bound gives
$$N_{s+2}(v)^2 =\sum_k\frac{(1+|k|^2)^{s+2}}{a_k^2}|\widehat f(k)|^2 \le m^{-2}N_s(f)^2.$$
The lower bound makes the coefficient sequence square-summable with weight
$(1+|k|^2)^{s+2}$; [F5] then gives $v\in H^{s+2}$, with
$\mathcal A v=f$. If $\mathcal A v=0$, then $a_k\widehat v(k)=0$ for every
$k$, hence all coefficients vanish and $v=0$. This proves surjectivity,
injectivity and the asserted inverse bound for every integer $s\ge2$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty smooth three-manifold without boundary that is
**compact**: for every family $(U_a)_{a\in A}$ of open subsets of $\Sigma$
with $\Sigma=\bigcup_{a\in A}U_a$, there is a finite subset $F\subseteq A$
such that $\Sigma=\bigcup_{a\in F}U_a$. In this item, “vacuum” means that the stress-energy tensor is zero and the
cosmological constant is fixed at $\Lambda=0$. Let $\widetilde h$ be a smooth
Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\widetilde\sigma$ be a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor field, let $\tau\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and let
$\phi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\phi(p)>0$ at every $p\in\Sigma$.
Use the positive scalar $\phi$ as a dimensionless conformal factor.

Write $\widetilde D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $\widetilde h$ and
$D$ for that of the metric $h$ defined below. On covariant tensor fields, these
symbols also denote their induced product connections, with the dual and
tensor-factor rules of the product-connection supplier in Definition references.
In a chart, $\widetilde h^{ij}$
denotes the inverse matrix to $\widetilde h_{ij}$. It is smooth because
$\det(\widetilde h_{ij})>0$ and the matrix inverse is the adjugate divided by
the determinant. For any smooth Riemannian metric $m$ on $\Sigma$, with
Levi-Civita connection $D^m$, define
$$R^m(X,Y)Z:=D^m_XD^m_YZ-D^m_YD^m_XZ-D^m_{[X,Y]}Z.$$
In a chart, $R[m]^a{}_{bij}$ denotes the components of
$R^m(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_b$. Define
$\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}:=R[m]^k{}_{ikj}$ and
$R(m):=m^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}$. In particular,
$\widetilde R:=R(\widetilde h)$, with the same curvature sign convention.
Define the scalar Laplacian by
$$\widetilde\Delta f:=\widetilde h^{ij} (\partial_i\partial_j f-\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k f),$$
where $\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ are the Christoffel symbols of
$\widetilde D$, given by the Levi-Civita Christoffel formula
in Definition references.
The curvature sign is the one displayed above. All traces, norms, raising of
indices and contractions in this item use the metric indicated by the
subscript. In particular,
$$\operatorname{tr}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma:=\widetilde h^{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{ij},\qquad |\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde h^{j\ell}\widetilde\sigma_{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma)_j:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde D_i\widetilde\sigma_{kj}.$$
The tensor $\widetilde\sigma$ is **transverse-traceless** (TT) with respect
to $\widetilde h$ when it is symmetric and both displayed trace and divergence
vanish. The input tensor in this definition is required to be TT.

Define
$$h:=\phi^4\widetilde h,\qquad K:=\phi^{-2}\widetilde\sigma+\frac{\tau}{3}h.$$
Because $\phi>0$, $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric; because
$\widetilde\sigma$ and $h$ are symmetric, $K$ is a smooth symmetric tensor.
Here $h$ is the candidate induced Riemannian metric and $K$ is the candidate
second fundamental form, with the library convention
$K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X n,Y)$ when the data are induced by a spacelike hypersurface
with future unit normal $n$. The pair is **vacuum conformal constraint data**.
It is abstract data on $\Sigma$; no embedding into a spacetime is part of this
definition. For its embedded Lorentzian interpretation assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the supplied smooth tangent-bundle
convention; the algebraic tensor definitions themselves use no choice
principle. Define the $h$-trace, squared norm and divergence by
$$\operatorname{tr}_hK:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|_h^2:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)_j:=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}.$$
With $R(h)$ computed using $h$, define the Hamiltonian and momentum residuals
$$\mathcal H(h,K):=R(h)+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2,\qquad \mathcal M_j(h,K):=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}-D_j(\operatorname{tr}_hK).$$
The data satisfy the vacuum constraint equations when
$\mathcal H(h,K)=0$ and $\mathcal M(h,K)=0$. For an embedded hypersurface,
these are the normal and normal-tangential Einstein constraints in the
specified $K$ convention.

Tensoriality of curvature and basis-independent contraction make these scalar
curvatures independent of the chart.
For dimensional bookkeeping in the SI length convention, $[\tau]=\mathrm m^{-1}$,
$[R(h)]=[\widetilde R]=[|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2]
=[\widetilde\Delta]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $[\phi]=1$. Thus all terms in the
scalar constraint equation have units $\mathrm m^{-2}$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of maps
$u:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb R^N$ whose pullbacks
$\widetilde u:=u\circ q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ are smooth;
these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when $N=1$).
Equivalently every smooth map $\widetilde u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$
that is $2\pi$-periodic in each coordinate descends to the unique map
$u([x])=\widetilde u(x)$, since periodicity makes this value independent of
$x$ in its equivalence class. For an integer $m\ge0$, define
$C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ similarly by requiring
$\widetilde u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$
([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), and define
$D^\alpha u([x]):=D^\alpha\widetilde u(x)$ for $|\alpha|\le m$.
Derivatives of a periodic $C^m$ map are periodic, so these values are
well-defined, with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}|(D^\alpha u)(x)|,$$
where the multi-index derivative is that of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]].

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when the representative $G(t,x,u):=F(t,q(x),u)$ is
locally the restriction of a smooth Euclidean map: for every
$(t,x,u)\in I\times\mathbb R^3\times O$ there are an open neighborhood
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^{4+m}$ and $\widetilde G\in C^\infty(V;\mathbb R^{m'})$
with $\widetilde G=G$ on $V\cap(I\times\mathbb R^3\times O)$.
For open $I$ this is the ordinary Euclidean definition. For nonopen $I$
it is the local extension convention at included endpoints, also admitting
a singleton interval. On a nondegenerate interval endpoint time derivatives
are the limits of interior derivatives; on a singleton no time derivative
is specified without choosing an extension. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge0$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

**(a)** Let $u\in H^s$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\alpha|\le s$. Then
$D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$ and
$$\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\,\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3),\qquad (ik)^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3(ik_j)^{\alpha_j}.$$

**(b)** Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy $N_s(u)<\infty$.
Then $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$, and there are constants
$0<c_s\le C_s<\infty$, depending only on $s$, such that
$$c_s\,N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le C_s\,N_s(u)^2 .$$
The right-hand inequality holds for every $u\in H^s$, so the two norms are
equivalent on $H^s$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(h,K)$ be the vacuum conformal constraint data of the definition. Then
$\operatorname{tr}_hK=\tau$ and the momentum residual vanishes:
$$\mathcal M_j(h,K)=0.$$
The Hamiltonian residual is
$$\mathcal H(h,K)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -8\widetilde\Delta\phi+\widetilde R\,\phi-|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2\phi^{-7} +\frac{2}{3}\tau^2\phi^5=0.$$
The displayed scalar equation is the **Lichnerowicz equation** for these
constant-mean-curvature (CMC) vacuum data. Here CMC means that the trace
$\operatorname{tr}_hK$ is spatially constant; its value is $\tau$.

$\mathcal C(\phi)=-8\widetilde\Delta\phi+\widetilde R\phi-
|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2\phi^{-7}+(2/3)\tau^2\phi^5$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Suppose the conformal metric has $\widetilde R=0$ and
$|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2=A$ is a positive constant, with constant
$\tau\ne0$. Then the Lichnerowicz equation has exactly one positive constant
solution,
$$\phi_0=\left(\frac{3A}{2\tau^2}\right)^{1/12}.$$
With a fixed length unit, $[A]=[\tau^2]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, so $\phi_0$ is
dimensionless. Uniqueness is only among positive constant solutions; no
uniqueness claim is made for arbitrary positive functions.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.
